title: Whether The Legal Demand Notice Was ... vs . on 16 May, 2011
full_text: Whether The Legal Demand Notice Was ... vs . on 16 May, 2011 IN THE COURT OF SH.SUSHIL ANUJ TYAGI METROPOLITAN MAGISTRATE: DWARKA COURT:NEW DELHI CC No. 10344/09 IN THE MATTER OF: Cholamandalam DBS Finance Ltd. Having its Registered Office at: 'Dare House', No.2, N.S.C. Bose Road, Parrys, Chennai ­600 001 ... Complainant. Vs. Sh. Parmanand R/o H.No. 923, Shiv Mandir, Wazirabad Near Fine Tallers, Gali no. 17, New Delhi ­110054 ... Accused Date of institution of case : 07.01.2009 Date of reserving Judgment : 05.05.2011 Date of pronouncement : 16.05.2011 JUDGMENT 1. Serial No. of the case : 10344/2009 2. Name of the complainant : Cholamandalam DBS Finance Ltd. 3. Name of the accused : Sh. Parmanand 4. Offence complained of : S.138 N. I. Act, 1881 5. Plea of accused : Pleaded not guilty. 6. Final Order : Acquitted 7. Date of such order : 16.05.2011 CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 1/16 BRIEF FACTS AND REASONS FOR DECISION OF THE CASE 1. The complainant has filed the present complaint under section 138 Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881 (hereinafter referred to as " NI Act ") and the brief facts as per the complainant are that at the request of the accused, the accused was given a personal loan by the complainant vide loan agreement no. XSEGJHA00000192934. The accused has issued cheque bearing no. 026194 dated 05.11.2008 drawn on Corporation Bank for amount of Rs. 28572, to the complainant towards partial discharge of legally enforceable debt and/or liability which got dishonoured on presentation for the reason "Insufficient Funds" vide return memo dated 06.11.2008. Thereafter, the complainant sent legal notice dt. 25.11.2008 to the accused vide speed post on 25.11.2008 and despite service the accused did not paid the cheque amount within 15 days of the receipt of legal demand notice. Hence the present complaint was filed against the accused by the complainant through its authorised representative on 07.01.2009 (hereinafter referred to as "AR"). 2. The AR was examined under section 200 Code of Criminal Procedure (hereinafter referred to as " CrPC ") by way of tendering of pre­ summoning affidavit. 3. After being satisfied that prima facie ingredients of Section 138 NI Act are made out, cognizance was taken and accused was summoned under section 204 CrPC. CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 2/16 4. After appearance of the accused the notice under section 251 CrPC was served on the accused to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. Accused admitted his signatures on the impugned cheque but also denied receiving of the legal demand notice in admission/denial proceedings under section 294 CrPC. 5. In Complainant's evidence, the AR (CW 1) tendered affidavit in post­summoning evidence as Ex CW 1/2 and relied on following documents: Ex CW1/A­1 ­Power of attorney Ex CW1/3 ­Board resolution Ex CW1/B ­Cheque in question Ex CW1/C ­Return memo Ex CW1/D ­Legal notice Ex CW1/E ­Postal receipt Ex CW1/F1 ­Complaint 6. The CW1 was examined, cross­examined and discharged. The Complainant evidence was closed. 7. The accused was examined under section 313 CrPC where all the incriminating evidence was put to the accused. Accused admitted the personal loan from the complainant however disputed the loan amount. Accused raised a defence that he was not told about the amount of loan sanctioned to him and blank cheques were taken from him for security. It was stated that he only knows hindi and the impugned cheque was signed in hindi however the rest of the body of the cheque was filled in english CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 3/16 which he does not know. Accused wished not to lead defence evidence and the case was accordingly fixed for final arguments. 8. In final arguments, the learned counsel for the complainant submitted that the accused was granted a loan of Rs. 44000 and the accused had issued a cheque of Rs. 28572 to repay the loan. It is further submitted that the address mentioned on the legal demand notice is the correct address of the accused and the accused has not disputed the said address or that he is not residing at the said address. It is further submitted that the presumption u/s 27 General Clauses Act is against the accused. It is alleged that since the accused has not led DE and has only stated u/s 313 CrPC, the presumptions under section 139 / 118 NI Act are not rebutted as statement u/s 313 is not evidence. Reliance was placed on V. S. Yadav v. Reena (Crl.A. No.1136 of 2010 decided by Hon'ble Delhi High court on 21.09.2010). It is further alleged that even if the cheque is issued as blank with signatures, the accused has given authority to the holder to fill in the details according to section 20 NI Act. The learned counsel for the complainant also relied on Rangappa v. Sri Mohan 2010 STPL(DC) 952 SC and submitted that it is held that once the accused admits the signatures on the cheque, the initial presumption as contemplated u/s 139 has to be raised by the courts. 9. On the other hand, the learned counsel for the accused contended that the complainant has failed to proved his case as the initial burden in CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 4/16 on the complainant which he must discharge in every criminal case. It is further submitted that it is not necessary for the accused to lead DE as the complainant case does not stands on his own footing. It is further contended that even the complainant be punished in the present case and a precedent be set so that such unlawful acts are not repeated. It is strongly argued that the accused knows only hindi and as clear from the cheque the body is filled in english language and in different inks. It is further alleged that the cheque is filled in different inks and it is clear that it is not filled by the accused. If the accused would have filled or got it filled it would have been in the same ink in which the signatures are put. It is further contended that during the cross­examination of CW­1 , CW­1 has failed to tell that who has received the cheques from the accused. It is further submitted that the accused was given loan by provocation and he is illiterate. It is submitted that the loan amount was not told to the accused and he was disbursed only Rs. 30,000­35,000 and blank signed cheques were taken for security purpose. The complainant had filled the blank cheques and without intimating the accused presented it. It is further contended that the accused has no liability towards the cheque in question. 10. Now, this court has carefully heard the rival contentions from both the sides and perused the judicial record. The following questions has levelled up for consideration of this court: CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 5/16 1. Whether the legal demand notice was served on the accused? 2. Whether the cheques were issued towards legally enforceable liability and consideration? Question no.1 11. In the present case, the legal demand notice EX CW1/D was sent through speed post. The speed post receipt EX CW1/E is filed on record. No proof of delivery is present on record. It is well settled law that the offence under section 138 would be constituted only when the legal demand notice is received by the accused and he has not made the payment within the stipulated period. The sending of notice is not same as receipt of notice. In this situation, the question arises is whether the accused had received the legal demand notice as required u/s 138 NI Act. To my mind, the answer is in affirmative. The reasons for this is that to attract offence u/s 138 , it is not necessary to prove actual service as the accused may be deemed served in certain cases. The presumption u/s 27 General Clauses Act, 1897 is against the accused. Section 27 General Clauses Act, 1897 is reproduced below: "27. Meaning of service by post. Where any Central Act or Regulation made after the commencement of this Act authorizes or requires any document to be served by post, whether the expression serve or either of the expressions give or send or any other expression is used, then, unless a different intention appears, the service shall be deemed to be effected by properly addressing, prepaying and posting by registered post, a letter CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 6/16 containing the document, and, unless the contrary is proved, to have been effected at the time at which the letter would be delivered in the ordinary course of post." 12. In C.C. Alavi Haji Appellant V. Palapetty Muhammed & Anr. Respondents 2007 STPL(DC) 952 SC, it was observed that the service of notice is presumpted until such presumption is rebutted by the addressee by proving to the contrary. It was held: "14. Section 27 gives rise to a presumption that service of notice has been effected when it is sent to the correct address by registered post. In view of the said presumption, when stating that a notice has been sent by registered post to the address of the drawer, it is unnecessary to further aver in the complaint that in spite of the return of the notice unserved, it is deemed to have been served or that the addressee is deemed to have knowledge of the notice. Unless and until the contrary is proved by the addressee, service of notice is deemed to have been effected at the time at which the letter would have been delivered in the ordinary course of business. This Court has already held that when a notice is sent by registered post and is returned with a postal endorsement "refused" or "not available in the house" or "house locked" or "shop closed" or "addressee not in station", due service has to be presumed. [ Vide Jagdish Singh Vs. Natthu Singh , AIR 1992 SC 1604, State of M.P. Vs. Hiralal & Ors. (1996) 7 SCC 523 and V. Raja Kumari Vs. P. Sub­barama Naidu & Anr. (2004) 8 SCC 774]. It is, therefore, manifest that in view of the presumption available under Section 27 of the Act, it is not necessary to aver in the complaint under Section 138 of the Act that service of notice was evaded by the accused or that the accused had a role to play, in the return of the notice unserved." It was further observed that even if the accused claims that he did not CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 7/16 received the legal demand notice, he may have paid the cheque amount within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court but if he fails, he cannot contend that he has not received the legal demand notice. The relevant extract is reproduced below: "17. It is also to be borne in mind that the requirement of giving of notice is a clear departure from the rule of Criminal Law, where there is no stipulation of giving of a notice before filing a complaint. Any drawer who claims that he did not receive the notice sent by post, can, within 15 days of receipt of summons from the court in respect of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, make payment of the cheque amount and submit to the Court that he had made payment within 15 days of receipt of summons (by receiving a copy of complaint with the summons) and, therefore, the complaint is liable to be rejected. A person who does not pay within 15 days of receipt of the summons from the Court along with the copy of the complaint under Section 138 of the Act, cannot obviously contend that there was no proper service of notice as required under Section 138 , by ignoring statutory presumption to the contrary under Section 27 of the G.C. Act and Section 114 of the Evidence Act. In our view, any other interpretation of the proviso would defeat the very object of the legislation. As observed in Bhaskaran's case (supra), if the "giving of notice" in the context of Clause (b) of the proviso was the same as the "receipt of notice" a trickster cheque drawer would get the premium to avoid receiving the notice by adopting different strategies and escape from legal consequences of Section 138 of the Act." 13. Thus, from the above observations it is crystal clear that when a registered letter is sent to the correct address, it is deemed to be served upon the addressee in the ordinary course. Thus even in absence of any CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 8/16 proof of delivery, the service of legal demand notice is presumed in the present case. The burden was on the accused to rebut the said presumption. The accused has not disputed the address mentioned on the legal demand notice nor he has stated that he is not residing at the said address. The perusal of bail bond reveals that the address mentioned therein is the same address as present on the legal demand notice. It is only contended that he has not received the notice but not led any evidence to prove the same. Thus, it can be safely concluded that the accused has failed to rebut the aforesaid presumption. Therefore this court holds that the accused was served with the legal demand notice as envisaged by S.138 NI Act. Question no.2 14. As far as the question of legally enforceable liability is concerned, it is important to discuss the law relating to Section 138 before proceeding to decide the present matter. Section 138 NI Act is reproduced below: "138. Dishonour of cheque for insufficiency, etc., of funds in the accounts Where any cheque drawn by a person on an account maintained by him with a banker for payment of any amount of money to another person from out of that account for the discharge, in whole or in part, of any debt or other liability, is returned by the bank unpaid, either because of the amount of money standing to the credit of that account is insufficient to honour the cheque or that it exceeds the amount arranged to be paid from that account by an agreement made with that CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 9/16 bank, such person shall be deemed to have committed an offence and shall without prejudice to any other provisions of this Act, be punished with imprisonment for "a term which may extend to two year", or with fine which may extend to twice the amount of the cheque, or with both: Provided that nothing contained in this section shall apply unless­ (a) The cheque has been presented to the bank within a period of six months from the date on which it is drawn or within the period of its validity, whichever is earlier. (b) The payee or the holder induce course of the cheque, as the case may be, makes a demand for the payment of the said amount of money by giving a notice, in writing, to the drawer, of the cheque, "within thirty days" of the receipt of information by him from the bank regarding the return of the cheques as unpaid, and (c) The drawer of such cheque fails to make the payment of the said amount of money to the payee or, as the case may be, to the holder in due course of the cheque, within fifteen days of the receipt of the said notice. Explanation: For the purpose of this section, "debt or other liability" means a legally enforceable debt or other liability." [Emphasis added] 15. The NI Act raises a rebuttable presumption under section 139 NI Act and 118 NI Act against the accused and in favour of the holder of cheque. 16. Section 139 NI Act reads: "139. Presumption in favour of holder It shall be presumed, unless the Contrary is proved, that the holder of a cheque received the cheque of the nature referred to in section 138 for the discharge, in whole or in part, or any debt or other liability." [Emphasis added] 17 Section 118 NI Act reads: "118. Presumptions as to negotiable instruments of CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 10/16 consideration Until the contrary is proved, the following presumptions shall be made: ­ (h) Of consideration: that every negotiable instrument was made or drawn for consideration, and that every such instrument, when it has bee accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred, was accepted, endorsed, negotiated or transferred for consideration. ........................................................................" [Emphasis added] 18. The accused may rebut the presumptions u/s 139 NI Act & u/s 118 NI Act by leading evidence or by showing preponderance of probabilities. In the present case, the accused had not examined himself as defence witness nor has he examined any other witness to prove his case. The accused has disputed the loan amount and has taken a defence that the cheque was issued as blank for security which the complainant has misused. Surprisingly, the CW­1 during the cross­examination has failed to answer the basic questions put by the learned counsel for accused. The relevant statements are as follows: "........The loan was sanctioned for an amount of Rs. 44,000 but I do not know the exact date of sanctioning of loan and who has sanctioned the loan.........I do not know how many EMIs were paid and what was the outstanding amount at the time of filing of complaint..........I do not know the cheque which was dishonoured was given to whom and CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 11/16 when......" The accused has disputed the loan amount and the liability under the impugned cheque. No loan agreement or statement of account has been filed on record. It was admitted by the CW­1 that the loan was repayable in 36 EMIs of Rs. 2381. When the EMI was of Rs.2381 then why the accused has issued the impugned cheque of Rs 28, 572 remains a mystical question in absence of any evidence suggesting settlement or payment after foreclosure of the loan account. The CW­1 has failed to answer to whom the cheque was handed over by the accused. It was stated by CW­1 during cross­examination that: "..........I do not know the cheque which was dishonoured by given to whom and when. I cannot say whether 3­4 security cheques are taken at the time of sanctioning of loan......." The complainant has not suggested as to how and when the cheque was issued by the accused to the the complainant. It is not proved whether the cheque was issued after some settlement or foreclosure of the loan. The CW­1 failed to answer the question regarding the liability of the accused on the date of filing of complaint and number of paid EMIs, during his cross­examination. No statement of account or loan agreement is placed on record to support the prosecution case. The fact that the impugned cheque is signed in hindi in different ink while the rest of cheque body filled in English in different inks supports the defence version. In the CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 12/16 shadow of these facts and circumstances, the presumption of legally enforceable liability and consideration in favour of the complainant stands rebutted. 19. The contention on behalf of the complainant that even if the cheque was issued in blank, it is given with authority u/s 20 NI Act to the complainant to fill and present it, does not appear convincing to this court. The section 20 NI Act reads: "20. Inchoate stamped instruments Where one person signs and delivers to another a paper stamped in accordance with the law relating to negotiable instruments then in force in [India], and either wholly blank or having written thereon an incomplete negotiable instrument, he thereby gives prima facie authority to the holder thereof to make or complete, as the case may be, upon it a negotiable instrument, for any amount specified therein and not exceeding the amount covered by the stamp. The person so signing shall be liable upon such instrument, in the capacity in which he signed the same, to any holder in due course for such amount; provided that no person other than a holder in due course shall recover from the person delivering the instrument anything in excess of the amount intended by him to be paid thereunder." [Emphasis added] It provides that even if the cheque is issued in blank it is given with express or implied prima facie authority to the holder to fill it. In the present case, there is no express authority is proved by the complainant. As far as the implied authority is concerned, the fact whether the authority was CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 13/16 given impliedly or not has to be gathered from the facts and circumstances of the case. There is nothing on record to suggest impliedness of authority except the signatures on the cheque. There is no evidence as to oral or written agreement as to why the present cheque was issued. There is also no evidence whether it is in pursuance of some settlement or agreement. Nothing on record infers as to when, how and to whom the accused has handed over the cheque and with what intention. Section 20 NI Act does not by itself give unbridled power to the holder of blank cheque. The intention of the parties surely has an important role to play. If the blank signed cheque is handed over to the holder without any mutual understanding as to the terms of presenting the cheque, it cannot be filled by the holder according to his own whims and fancies and make the signatory liable for the amount filled. Even if a blank cheque is filled by the holder, then it must be according to the prior understanding between the parties as to filling of the cheque and there must be at least a prior intimation to the drawer. In the present case there appears to be none. In these circumstances, this court is of the view that the provisions under section 20 NI Act is of no benefit to the complainant. 20. It is rightly contended on behalf of the complainant that the statement under section 313 CrPC is no evidence. However, the law is CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 14/16 now crystallised on the point that it is not necessary for the accused to lead defence evidence in criminal prosecution. It is a trite in law that the prosecution case must stand on its own legs and it is not for the accused but the prosecution who has the burden to prove his case beyond reasonable doubt. The burden on the accused is not as high as it is on the prosecution. The burden on the prosecution is to prove their case beyond any doubts while the burden on the accused is to raise improbabilities in prosecution case or cast doubts. The accused has a right of silence and he is under no obligation to lead defence evidence. The accused may discharge his burden by shaking the prosecution case and showing preponderence of probabilities in his favour. Any benefit of doubt obviously goes to the accused. In the present case, the accused has validly discharged his burden by creating dents in prosecution story and has raised material probabilities in his favour. After rebuttal of complainant favouring presumptions, the onus shifts and it is imperative on the complainant to prove his case beyond reasonable doubts, which the complainant has miserably failed to do. FINAL ORDER 21. In view of above discussions and observations, this court holds that the complainant has failed in proving their case beyond the shadow of reasonable doubts. This court exonerates the accused Parmanand for the CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 15/16 offence under section 138 NI Act. The accused is hereby acquitted. Bail bonds are cancelled and sureties stands discharged. Endorsements, if any, stands cancelled. 22. File be consigned to the record room after completion of necessary formalities. Announced in the open Court on 16th of May, 2011 (Sushil Anuj Tyagi) Metropolitan Magistrate Dwarka, New Delhi 16.05.2011 CC No. 10344/09 Cholamandalam Vs. Parmanand Page no. 16/16
